prior_art.basis: Independent review by claude-independent-prior-art-reviewer-20261106: Pressure-sensing implants exist in small studies but no one has shown they stop glaucoma, so the Main KPI of 76,000,000 patients protected is open work. The EYEMATE-SC suprachoroidal telemetric sensor has been implanted in 24 patients with three-year follow-up: no dislocation, position drift from 1.6 to 2.1 millimetres over 1,080 days, no astigmatic effect, good agreement with Goldmann tonometry, high adherence, 15 moderate adverse events with one possibly sensor-related, and the authors state the effect on progression and quality of life needs further study; a 2026 review lists Eyemate-IO, Eyemate-SC, IOP Connect and Q Smart with cost, regulatory approval and long-term validation as open barriers (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=%28%22eyemate%22%20OR%20%22intraocular%20pressure%20sensor%22%29%20AND%20implant%20AND%20glaucoma&format=json&pageSize=5&resultType=core). The registry confirms the scale: ARGOS-IO in 16 and ARGOS-SC in 24 patients, the rest contact-lens sensors. The harder half is that pressure control alone does not stop the disease: a 2026 study found 19 percent of eyes progressing fast despite office pressure at target, and reviews state neurodegeneration often persists after pressure lowering. Open code is eight small monitoring apps and non-contact prototypes (https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=glaucoma+intraocular+pressure+monitoring&per_page=10&sort=stars). Honest limit: implanted telemetric pressure sensing is already demonstrated prior art, so a sensor-only task is a known answer; the open work is turning continuous pressure data into prevented blindness. (open solution found: no; known answer: no; 6 project-level searches of api.github.com/search/repositories, export.arxiv.org/api/query, api.crossref.org/works; draft 1b6cf6cb2d4ba33efbbbf3ef6ae983dcf8022457d2d466e87f3fe3d57d72b03f, source 63c41fb0557d6ea77ace4f929a50ed53a71dcb5ddb97bbde82a681effe48e0e4)
